nodes.question: How do we build reliable physical electronic systems from signals, devices, power, measurements and control?
nodes.why: A circuit can be logically right yet fail electrically, under transient loads, during measurement, or in a real PCB layout.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Separate signal representation, operating point, parasitics/physical return, regulation, power conversion, thermal/safety and measurement contracts. The three books are complementary, not substitutes.

nodes.question: What physical laws does a circuit actually exploit?
nodes.why: Voltage/current abstractions conceal real reference choices, impedance, energy storage and unintended current loops.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: The Art of Electronics Chapter 1 develops voltage, current, impedance and passive behavior as an engineering vocabulary; the same quantities govern both high-speed traces and switching converter currents.

nodes.question: When is a transistor a switch, an amplifier, or a current source?
nodes.why: A device operating region and external load/feedback determine realized behavior.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Horowitz/Hill Chs. 2–3 cover BJT/FET switches, amplifiers and current mirrors; Erickson/Maksimović Ch. 4 treats power switches under voltage/current, speed, conduction and switching-loss constraints.

nodes.question: Why can a feedback amplifier perform precise tasks but still oscillate or distort?
nodes.why: Finite gain, bandwidth, saturation, loading and phase shift limit the feedback idealization.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: The Art of Electronics Ch. 4 covers real op-amp behavior and Ch. 5 precision amplifiers. Useful circuit-level performance depends on source impedance, feedback dynamics, supply and the selected IC.

nodes.question: Why does the same sensor signal look much noisier after amplification?
nodes.why: Different noise contributions scale with source impedance, bandwidth and circuit gain.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: The Art of Electronics Ch. 8 describes input voltage noise, input current noise interacting with source resistance and Johnson noise of that resistance. These contributions must be combined with actual bandwidth and correlation assumptions.

source_sections.section: Ch. 8 §8.3.1 Voltage noise; op-amp noise discussion

technical_distinctions.mechanism: Source impedance converts current noise into voltage and must be considered with Johnson noise.
technical_distinctions.discriminating_observation: Vary source resistance/bandwidth and compare measured noise to device noise density and noise gain.

unresolved_questions: Which component tolerances, actual physical topology and operating conditions would invalidate this explanation?

nodes.question: Can the oscilloscope probe itself create or conceal an electronic failure?
nodes.why: A probe adds impedance and creates a ground-loop antenna; observed ringing can be measurement-induced.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Johnson/Graham Ch. 3 §3.4 examines probe loading and grounding; long probe return loops pick up magnetic noise. Measurement must establish whether a waveform persists with a small appropriate reference loop.

source_sections.section: Ch. 3 §3.4 How Probes Load Down a Circuit

technical_distinctions.mechanism: A long ground lead and loaded node create a measurement-dependent waveform.
technical_distinctions.discriminating_observation: Repeat with short local return, differential probe or alternate method without accidentally changing circuit conditions.

nodes.question: Why does a simple linear regulator run hot while a switcher can be noisy?
nodes.why: A linear pass device burns its input-output voltage drop at full load current; a switcher transfers energy through reactive storage but adds switch-frequency ripple and EMI.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: The Art of Electronics §9.6.1 explicitly gives the dissipated pass-element power as load current times its voltage drop and contrasts the linear regulator with more efficient but more complex switching regulators.

technical_distinctions.contrast: Pass-device loss versus switched energy transfer
technical_distinctions.mechanism: Linear dissipation follows voltage drop times current, while switching can reduce power loss at the cost of ripple and complexity.
technical_distinctions.discriminating_observation: Compute and measure total efficiency and output noise at the actual load.

unresolved_questions: Which component tolerances, actual physical topology and operating conditions would invalidate this explanation?

nodes.question: How does switching produce a different average output voltage?
nodes.why: Duty-dependent inductor volt-seconds and capacitor charge determine steady-state behavior under a small-ripple assumption.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Fundamentals of Power Electronics Ch. 2 develops volt-second and charge balance and explicitly decomposes the output into DC plus switching ripple. Small-ripple is a useful approximation, not a claim that instantaneous output is constant.

technical_distinctions.mechanism: Volt-second/charge balance establish periodic average behavior; real output retains switching harmonics.
technical_distinctions.discriminating_observation: Identify switching period and check the small-ripple approximation against measured current/voltage ripple.

unresolved_questions: Which component tolerances, actual physical topology and operating conditions would invalidate this explanation?

nodes.question: What distinguishes buck, boost, buck-boost, flyback and bridge converters?
nodes.why: The switching network, energy-storage path and isolation requirements determine the reachable conversion ratio and stresses.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Erickson/Maksimović Chs. 5–6 map continuous/discontinuous modes, topological transformations and isolated converter forms. A simplified DC transformation does not settle switch ratings, losses or control behavior.

nodes.mechanism_explanation: Fundamentals of Power Electronics Chs. 3–4 model copper/semiconductor losses and switching behavior; device capacitance, reverse recovery, winding loss and thermal paths change realized efficiency.

nodes.mechanism_explanation: Power Electronics Ch. 5 isolates discontinuous conduction mode and its boundary; the averaged continuous-conduction model cannot be carried across that boundary unmodified.

nodes.mechanism_explanation: Power Electronics Chs. 7–9 derive averaged dynamics, transfer functions and controller compensation; real loop response must account for the plant and measured gain/phase margins.

nodes.question: Why can a comparatively slow digital clock require high-frequency PCB engineering?
nodes.why: Interconnect behavior depends on voltage edge rise time relative to propagation delay along the conductor, not only on bit rate.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: High-Speed Digital Design §1.3 contrasts a physically short line whose voltage is almost uniform with a longer line showing a propagating edge over different positions.

technical_distinctions.mechanism: A 'slow' clock may generate subnanosecond transitions whose spatial edge length is short relative to PCB wiring.
technical_distinctions.discriminating_observation: Compare trace propagation delay with the edge rise time, not only the clock period.

nodes.question: Why does a voltage edge bounce along an ordinary-looking wire?
nodes.why: A distributed interconnect has impedance and propagation delay, and load/source mismatches reflect incident waves.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: High-Speed Digital Design Ch. 4 develops transmission lines, input/load impedance and reflection behavior. Geometry, termination and return plane must be considered as one physical link.

nodes.question: What exactly changes when I terminate a fast digital signal at the source?
nodes.why: Source impedance matched to line impedance absorbs returning waves and prevents repeated reflections at that end; the far end and intermediate taps can still behave differently.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Johnson/Graham §4.3.3 describes source termination, including the half-amplitude initial launched step and far-end doubling in a particular open-end configuration. Source termination is not a universal fix for every branching trace.

technical_distinctions.contrast: Matched launch versus matched receiving end
technical_distinctions.mechanism: Source termination absorbs returning reflections; in an open-ended line the full-level arrival follows a different wave sequence.
technical_distinctions.discriminating_observation: Measure at both source and far end; don't conclude from one oscilloscope location.

nodes.question: Why does cutting a ground plane hurt a trace even if the trace itself is intact?
nodes.why: At fast edge rates the return path minimizes loop inductance and concentrates under the signal; crossing a plane gap increases loop area and coupling.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Johnson/Graham §5.1 explains the high-frequency signal-return current's preference for low-inductance paths directly below the outgoing trace, rather than low-DC-resistance paths spread across a plane.

source_sections.section: Ch. 5 §5.1 High-Speed Current Follows Least Inductance

technical_distinctions.contrast: DC ground continuity versus high-frequency return path
technical_distinctions.mechanism: A continuous ohmic connection can have a large loop inductance for a fast edge.
technical_distinctions.discriminating_observation: Inspect a trace crossing a plane discontinuity versus one over continuous reference.

nodes.mechanism_explanation: High-Speed Digital Design Chs. 1, 5 and 9 detail coupling and PCB/connector paths. A signal line can meet its own impedance target yet still be corrupted by neighboring switching return currents.
